title: Dee Day

jokes.text: Mac, you have the tendon dexterity of a sow, so yes, it's necessary.
jokes.setup: Mac complains about Dennis's warmup exercises, asking if they're really necessary.
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers a hyper-specific, contemptuous insult comparing Mac's physical dexterity to a female pig, treating it as obvious fact.
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis: condescending, oddly specific, delivered as unchallengeable fact. 'Tendon dexterity of a sow' is a genuinely funny image. Character integration is high — this is Dennis's voice perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Mac, you have the tendon dexterity of a sow

jokes.text: Charlie doing the warm-up perfectly and Dennis saying 'Yes, very good, Charlie' like praising a golden retriever, then 'Needy and desperate for approval, but good.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is running the group through preparation drills and Charlie complies eagerly.
jokes.punchline: Dennis praises Charlie like a child, then immediately psychoanalyzes him — 'Needy and desperate for approval, but good' — undercutting the praise completely.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures Dennis's narcissistic mentor posture — he can't give a compliment without also diagnosing your pathology. The rhythm of praise-then-evisceration is tight and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Needy and desperate for approval, but, uh, good.

jokes.text: Mac does a thumbs-up gesture to signal confidence; Dennis says 'With one little gesture, he tells me everything I need to know. That wordless display of confidence earns my confidence.' Then immediately: 'Don't. I did it already. You're so desperate.'
jokes.setup: Mac tries to do a cool confident gesture to impress Dennis, thinking he's nailing it.
jokes.punchline: Dennis reads it as pathetic approval-seeking, and the moment Mac tries to do it again, Dennis shuts him down: 'You're so desperate.'
jokes.explanation: The joke works on the Mac/Dennis dynamic — Mac desperately wanting Dennis's approval, Dennis finding it repulsive. The double beat (Dennis reads it, then Mac immediately does it again) adds escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: With one little gesture, he tells me everything I need to know. That wordless display of confidence earns my confidence.

jokes.text: The 'world is our oyster' vs. 'world is our clam' shellfish debate that derails the entire planning meeting.
jokes.setup: Dennis gives an inspiring speech about seizing opportunity: 'The world is our oyster.'
jokes.punchline: The gang immediately derails into an extended debate about which shellfish is superior — clams, barnacles, abalone, mussels — completely forgetting the actual plan.
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny gang derailment. The escalation from oyster → clam → barnacle → abalone → mussels is funny precisely because each character contributes with total sincerity. Dennis's exasperated 'Let's not get into a whole thing' is the right button. Also plants the clam/shellfish running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Don't say 'oyster.' Say 'clam.'

jokes.text: Dee enters singing '♪ Uh, Dee is in the house ♪' — a full self-hype song — while the guys immediately say 'First things first, we got to ditch Dee.'
jokes.setup: Dee arrives with enormous energy, performing a hype entrance song for herself.
jokes.punchline: The gang's instant, unanimous, overlapping plan to ditch her cuts directly against her oblivious excitement.
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition is sharp: Dee's performed confidence against the gang's reflexive contempt. The hype song is a funny character choice — she wrote herself a theme — and the immediate 'Oh, shit. Yeah, let's ditch her' is a perfect deadpan counter. Strong scene opener.

jokes.text: Dee explains 'Dee Day' — for 24 hours the gang must do everything she says, and violations earn an extra day — while the guys try to cram in final insults before the deadline: 'Dee's a bird! You're a bird!'
jokes.setup: Dee announces Dee Day and begins counting down. The gang scrambles to squeeze in bird insults before the clock runs out.
jokes.punchline: Multiple characters shouting overlapping 'You're a bird!' insults in the final three seconds, with one coming in right at zero — 'You're a stupid—!'
jokes.explanation: Great comedic structure — the countdown creates urgency, and the gang's desperate scramble to insult Dee before the window closes is perfectly in character. The overlapping, panicked delivery escalates well and the final truncated insult is a great button.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: ♪ Uh, Dee is in the house ♪

jokes.text: Dee announces her first topic for the day: 'My feelings.'
jokes.setup: Dee has the floor for the first time, teasing that she's going to hold court the way the guys do with their grand monologues.
jokes.punchline: 'My first topic? My feelings.' — the deflation from their expectation of something ambitious to this emotionally vulnerable, sitcom-cliché topic.
jokes.explanation: Clean setup/punchline. The deflation works, though it's not a terribly surprising beat — the joke is functional and character-appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: First things first, we got to ditch Dee.

jokes.text: The gang's four simultaneous talking-head confessionals while Dee talks about her feelings: Dennis obsesses about the plan, Mac worries about Charlie outshining him, Charlie is trying to figure out if Dennis has candy, and Frank rants about clams.
jokes.setup: Dee is mid-monologue about her feelings, expecting the gang to listen.
jokes.punchline: Four intercut confessionals reveal each character is completely ignoring her and thinking about: (1) the plan, (2) Dennis's approval, (3) whether Dennis has candy, (4) shellfish preparation — with Charlie's being the most absurdly pure.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best structural jokes. The intercut confessionals perfectly reveal each character's internal monologue, and they're all beautifully in-character: Dennis narcissistically plots, Mac frets about Dennis's approval, Charlie is laser-focused on candy, and Frank is STILL on clams. The escalating specificity — especially Charlie deducing candy from a 'crinkle' sound and Frank's earnest clam preparation monologue — is exceptional character comedy. Rewatch value is high because every confessional is loaded.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, my God. You forgot. Oh, that makes it so much better.

jokes.text: Dennis's internal monologue interrupts Dee mid-feelings-speech: 'Today of all days, and now I'm being forced to listen to her feelings? I won't do it. And who cares about her feelings anyway? Nobody, that's who. What about my feelings? Now, that's interesting.'
jokes.setup: Dee begins earnestly sharing her feelings
jokes.punchline: Dennis's internal voice dismisses her entirely mid-sentence and pivots immediately to his own feelings as infinitely more interesting — a perfect window into his narcissism
jokes.explanation: This talking-head perfectly distills Dennis Reynolds as a character: the total incapacity to care about anyone but himself, the clinical self-importance ('What about my feelings? Now, that's interesting'). Character integration is near-perfect — this monologue could belong to no one else. Approaches an 8 on craft because it's pure character expression with strong economy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Dee's a bird!

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You're a bird!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I hate you, bird!

jokes.text: Frank's confessional: 'You know who eats raw shellfish? Seagulls, that's who. Clams you bake. Clams you fry. Pop a rubber band around them, stuff them full of bread, boil them shits for an hour. There's a million ways you can prepare a clam. Make the world your clam. Just sounds better.'
jokes.setup: Frank's confessional is supposedly about why he was distracted during Dee's speech.
jokes.punchline: Frank has spent the entire time thinking about clam preparation and concludes — with complete sincerity — that 'make the world your clam' is superior idiomatically. He also invokes seagulls eating raw shellfish, which ties Dee into it.
jokes.explanation: Frank's callback to the shellfish debate, delivered with the earnestness of a man who has genuinely been thinking this through, is delightful. 'Boil them shits for an hour' is Frank in one sentence. The seagull line connecting to Dee-as-bird is a subtle bonus.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Today, it's you who will be forced to sit and just listen. And my first topic? My feelings.

jokes.text: Charlie's confessional: 'I'm pretty sure Dennis has candy. I heard a crinkle in his pocket that sounded like the wrapper of a candy. I gave Mac a look to let him know that I figured out Dennis has candy. Hopefully, if we nail this plan, he'll give us some candy. I want that candy.'
jokes.setup: Charlie's confessional is supposed to explain what he was thinking during Dee's speech.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's entire inner monologue during the grand planning session has been exclusively devoted to detecting and wanting candy — with the investigation, the interpersonal signaling to Mac, the conditional hope — all with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comedic peak. Charlie's candy obsession is built with perfect internal logic — he HEARD a crinkle, he investigated, he signaled Mac, he has a conditional plan. The payoff when Dennis actually reveals the candy later (he uses it to manage Charlie) makes this retroactively even better. 'I want that candy' as the concluding statement — with Charlie's earnest delivery — is as funny as this show gets. Pure Charlie Kelly, perfectly economical, enormous rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Today of all days, and now I'm being forced to listen to her feelings? I won't do it. And who cares about her feelings anyway? Nobody, that's who.

jokes.text: Mac's confessional about why he's been off: 'Hey, why was Charlie outshining me earlier? I mean, what's that all about? It's like he wants something from Dennis. But what? Attention? Love? Why'd he throw me that look? Does he want to replace me? Is that what's going on? What the hell does he want?'
jokes.setup: Mac's confessional is meant to explain his distraction during Dee's speech.
jokes.punchline: Mac's inner monologue is entirely consumed by jealousy over Charlie getting Dennis's attention — a paranoid spiral about being replaced, mirroring the kind of anxious romance Mac has with Dennis.
jokes.explanation: Mac's jealousy over Dennis's attention is a long-running character truth, and his spiral here — reading into Charlie's look, fearing replacement — perfectly mirrors a romantic insecurity. Well-integrated character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Uh-oh. I'm forgetting my part of the plan with every second that goes by. Dennis is gonna yell at me again.

jokes.text: After Dee's speech, all four men respond with 'Yes, absolutely' and 'Everything you were saying, we were totally listening,' having clearly not heard a word she said.
jokes.setup: Dee finishes her feelings monologue and asks if they agree.
jokes.punchline: The gang responds with overlapping, over-eager agreement — 'Absolutely,' 'That's totally true,' 'Yeah, yeah, yeah' — without being able to repeat a word of what she said.
jokes.explanation: Functional payoff to the confessional sequence — confirms they heard nothing. A bit predictable but the overlapping eager agreement is performed well. Works as a button on joke #8.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm pretty sure Dennis has candy. I heard a crinkle in his pocket that sounded like the wrapper of a candy.

jokes.text: Dee announces she needs to 'take a quick squirt 'cause that beer just went right through me,' and the gang immediately switches to screaming into a pillow and planning to escape.
jokes.setup: The gang has been performing politeness all through Dee's speech. Dee exits for the bathroom.
jokes.punchline: The instant the door closes, the facade collapses: 'Goddamn bird!' 'Where's the scream pillow?' — confirming the whole polite act was entirely performative.
jokes.explanation: 'Where's the scream pillow?' implies this is a regular coping object, which is a great background detail. The speed of the personality switch is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Make the world your clam. Just sounds better.

jokes.text: Dennis's revised plan: everybody has to take a dump once in 24 hours, so each person will execute their part of the plan during their bathroom break.
jokes.setup: The gang despairs that Dee Day has derailed their elaborate plan.
jokes.punchline: Dennis solves the problem by building the entire new plan around the biological certainty of bowel movements — presenting this as a stroke of genius.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Dennis presenting bathroom logistics as tactical genius — his grandiosity applied to something scatological. It also sets up the running 'I have to take a shit' gag that pays off repeatedly.

dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah, yeah. Absolutely. Everything you were saying, we were totally listening.

jokes.text: Mac misunderstands 'it's time for Charlie to take his shit' as literally needing to poop, while Dennis and Charlie know it's the cover story for the plan. Mac helpfully asks 'Is there time?'
jokes.setup: Dennis tells Charlie it's time for 'his shit' — meaning his part of the plan.
jokes.punchline: Mac enthusiastically agrees Charlie should 'go poop,' completely missing the metaphor, while Dennis and Charlie exchange knowing looks.
jokes.explanation: Classic Mac being the dumbest in the room. The layering of literal vs. figurative 'shit' is light wordplay that works well enough.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I'm gonna go take a quick squirt 'cause that beer just went right through me

jokes.text: Dennis tells Charlie to 'keep this kind of good focus in mind when it comes to what's inside your pants, 'cause I want that, man... I want what's in your pants.'
jokes.setup: Dennis praises Charlie's focus and attention to detail for the plan.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's phrasing — 'what's inside your pants... I want what's in your pants' — sounds sexually suggestive but he's referring to some part of the plan hidden on Charlie's person. Mac's horrified 'No, no' punctuates it.
jokes.explanation: Light misdirection/double entendre. Works as a quick gag on Dennis's obliviousness to how he sounds, though it's not particularly deep.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: She just went to the bathroom. See, everybody's got to take a dump at least once in every 24-hour period.

jokes.text: Mac has to 'take a shit' next and immediately announces it in front of Dee. Dennis panics: 'No. What, now? No. Well, make up your mind, or I do the horn.'
jokes.setup: The plan requires each person to use their bathroom break as cover. Mac now says he has to go.
jokes.punchline: The elaborate coded scheme immediately falls apart as Mac can't resist announcing it plainly in front of Dee, and Dennis nearly breaks his composure.
jokes.explanation: Functional running gag — the plan immediately degrading because Mac can't be subtle. Gets the job done.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What? No, that's not what he's talking about, Mac. What he means is that it's time for me to go to the school, break in using my old janitor's key...

jokes.text: Charlie's failed scheme at the school — introducing himself by saying he 'got fired on account of a relationship I was having with a Juggalo child' and that he's 'ready to have new relationships with the children.'
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to charm the school nurse Terry into letting him use the office, explaining his history.
jokes.punchline: Charlie casually mentions he was fired for a 'relationship with a Juggalo child' and immediately says he's 'ready to have new relationships with the children' — deeply criminal framing delivered as cheerful icebreaker.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional dark comedy. 'Juggalo child' is a hyper-specific, absurd detail that makes the already-troubling admission somehow funnier. The immediate pivot to 'I'm ready to have new relationships with the children' — delivered with no self-awareness — is perfectly Charlie. High originality, high character integration, and the dark tone is fully earned by the show's established universe.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: And keep this kind of good focus in mind when it comes to what's inside your pants, 'cause I want that, man. I want what's in your pants.

jokes.text: Charlie shows Terry his old janitor's key to explain how he got in the building. Terry stares at it. Long beat. 'Oh. Right.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has broken into a school without permission and is trying to explain himself to the sitting nurse.
jokes.punchline: Terry's completely flat 'Oh. Right.' in response to Charlie producing a years-old janitor's key as justification. The understatement of the reaction to something deeply weird is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Terry's deadpan acceptance is funny — the 'Oh. Right.' suggests the bar for things making sense has been abandoned entirely. Economy is perfect: two syllables of acknowledgment does all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I got fired on account of a relationship I was having with a Juggalo child

jokes.text: Charlie tries to get Terry to leave by saying kids are breaking into his car. Terry: 'I ride a bike.' Charlie: 'Yeah, that's what I meant. They were breaking on in to your bicycle. Kicked it in half. Filled it with horse manure. Kind of a prank, I guess.'
jokes.setup: Charlie needs Terry to leave the room, so he invents an emergency involving Terry's vehicle.
jokes.punchline: Charlie smoothly pivots to the bicycle, then escalates the fictional vandalism to absurd specificity: 'Kicked it in half. Filled it with horse manure. Kind of a prank, I guess.' — the casual qualifier at the end is perfect.
jokes.explanation: Charlie improvising a lie in real-time and committing fully is a show staple done here with great escalation. 'Filled it with horse manure. Kind of a prank, I guess.' is the standout — the specificity of the horse manure, the casual shrug of 'kind of a prank.' This is quotable, well-structured, and pure Charlie energy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm ready to have new relationships with the children.

jokes.text: Terry comes back: 'My bike is fine.' Charlie: 'One step ahead of me, aren't you, Terry?'
jokes.setup: Charlie sends Terry outside to check on his supposedly vandalized bike.
jokes.punchline: Terry returns, bike totally fine, and Charlie's response — rather than being embarrassed — is to frame Terry as unusually clever: 'One step ahead of me, aren't you, Terry?'
jokes.explanation: Charlie refusing to accept failure and instead complimenting Terry as a master tactician is a great character beat. The economy is superb — it reframes defeat as respect, which is both absurd and very Charlie.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: They were breaking on in to your bicycle. Kicked it in half. Filled it with horse manure.

jokes.text: Charlie asks: 'Hey, can I use your phone and pretend to be you?' Terry: 'No.' Charlie: 'Okay. That's strike three on my count. I'm gonna fuck your bike up, Terry.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has failed at every angle of his plan and is running out of options.
jokes.punchline: He asks with complete sincerity if he can impersonate Terry on his own phone. After the flat refusal, Charlie announces — casually, like a professional — that he will now vandalize Terry's bike as promised.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes. The request to 'use your phone and pretend to be you' is so baldly stated it's almost conceptual art. Terry's flat 'No' is perfect. Then 'That's strike three on my count' gives Charlie a quasi-procedural dignity, and the pivot to 'I'm gonna fuck your bike up, Terry' — casual, resigned, almost professional — is a great button. The callback to his earlier horse manure threat makes this land even harder on rewatch.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Uh, I'm gonna fuck your bike up, Terry.

jokes.text: Mac shouts 'Shut up, Mac, you racist!' at himself while pointing at Mac to deflect blame onto him, then 'She's racist! She's the one that's racist! She's making us do it.'
jokes.setup: Charlie calls Mac racist for the costume/accent
jokes.punchline: Mac's defense is to simultaneously blame himself ('Shut up, Mac') and everyone else around him in a panicked loop
jokes.explanation: Mac shouting 'Shut up, Mac, you racist!' at himself is a good absurdist beat. The logic of using his own name in third person while panicking is funny but not sophisticated.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: It's insanely racist. We didn't want to do it, but you know, Dee's humor is so lowbrow.

jokes.text: Mac blaming the makeup for making him sick. Frank: 'It's not the makeup, Frank. It's the bag of clams you made us stop for before we came here.' Frank: 'The clam is fine.'
jokes.setup: Frank is visibly ill and blaming his theatrical makeup.
jokes.punchline: Mac correctly diagnoses it as the clams Frank insisted on eating before the scheme. Frank's response — 'The clam is fine.' — delivered with total conviction while presumably looking terrible, is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Perfect payoff to the shellfish running gag. Frank's sincere insistence 'The clam is fine' while clearly suffering from food poisoning is an absurd piece of denial comedy. Great economy — three words, all the information needed.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: That's why you suck at everything, Maxie. I say if you're gonna do a racist stereotype, you best do it right.

jokes.text: Frank: 'If we got a bag of oysters, those would've made us really sick.'
jokes.setup: Frank is defending his clam choice while clearly ill from the clams.
jokes.punchline: His defense of clams is that oysters would have been worse — delivered as wisdom while suffering from clam poisoning.
jokes.explanation: A great secondary beat on the clam gag — the oyster callback lands because we've heard Frank's pro-clam position all episode. His logic (oysters would have been worse) while actively ill is a beautiful piece of delusional character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I want you to ram him, all right? Nothing crazy, but it's got to be believable.

jokes.text: Mac's 'suggestion' for the valet plan: very carefully hinting that Frank should be the one to cause the car accident without saying why out loud — 'I'm not saying out loud why you should be the one to have the car accident, but I think it would play much better.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Frank need someone to fake a car accident to distract the valet.
jokes.punchline: Mac implies Frank — a small, old, visually comedic man — would be more believable in an accident without being willing to say it directly, tiptoeing around the unspoken 'you look pathetic' reason.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in what isn't said — Mac's elaborate diplomatic hedging around 'you look like you'd be more believable as an accident victim.' Frank accepting this graciously ('I do appreciate that you're working on your prejudices') adds another layer.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: It won't be the clams, because if it was clams... ...clams and I was sick, it would be all over the pavement.

jokes.text: Frank: 'I do appreciate that you're working on your prejudices, Frank. I, too, am trying to become a better man... but I just... I really think that, unfortunately, it is a better plan. It's a good plan.' Then: 'So I'm just gonna go ahead and do that.'
jokes.setup: Mac has gently suggested Frank cause the accident without saying why.
jokes.punchline: Frank responds as if this is a conversation about overcoming bias and personal growth — thanking Mac for 'working on his prejudices' — before agreeing that yes, it is a better plan, and walking off to crash a car.
jokes.explanation: The gap between the language used ('prejudices,' 'becoming a better man') and what's actually being agreed to (Frank will fake-crash a car because he looks pathetic) is funny. Frank's dignified acceptance is a good character note.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: It's not the clams!
Frank immediately vomits

jokes.text: Frank attempts to be the valet while visibly sick from the clams, explaining his appearance: 'It's just that I got a little skin thing going on. But I may get sick, but it won't be clams. It won't be the clams, because if it was clams, it would be all over the pavement.'
jokes.setup: Frank, in full theatrical makeup and visibly nauseated from clam poisoning, tries to impersonate a valet and take the councilwoman's car.
jokes.punchline: Frank's explanation for why he looks terrible is 'a skin thing,' and his insistence that whatever happens, it definitely won't be clams — delivered while clearly about to be very ill from clams.
jokes.explanation: Frank's escalating clam denial while actively succumbing to it is a great character bit — the more he insists it's not clams, the more obviously it is. 'It would be all over the pavement' as a hypothetical while standing next to this woman is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: It's not the clams!

jokes.text: Frank vomits (implied/visual), screaming 'It's not the clams!' as the councilwoman flees.
jokes.setup: Frank has been insisting throughout the episode that the clams are fine and he's not sick from clams.
jokes.punchline: Frank explosively vomits in front of the councilwoman while screaming 'It's not the clams! It don't make no sense!' — full physical payoff to the running denial.
jokes.explanation: Perfect payoff for the clam running gag — the full arc from shellfish debate to Frank insisting 'The clam is fine' to projectile vomiting while screaming 'It's not the clams!' is a structurally satisfying comedy escalation. The specificity of 'It don't make no sense!' adds to Frank's delusional commitment. High impact, deserved rewatch bonus.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: 'with the quivering lips of two souls desperate to taste the juices of passion.' Did that seem like that to you guys?

jokes.text: During Dee's play, someone sings the wrong lyric — 'your love is all I ever wanted to be' — and Dee snaps: '"For me," idiot.'
jokes.setup: The gang is performing Dee's original musical number under duress.
jokes.punchline: Someone flubs the lyric mid-performance; Dee's stage-director correction 'For me, idiot' — whispered from the wings — punctures the theatrical pretension.
jokes.explanation: Light gag, mostly functions as connective tissue. 'Idiot' as her note to her performer is very Dee. Quick and clean.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Plant one on me, Covington!
Forced romantic scene between Mac and Charlie

jokes.text: Dee's stage direction reads that the two characters kiss 'with the quivering lips of two souls desperate to taste the juices of passion.' Dee asks: 'Did that seem like that to you guys? No. Me neither. So do that, then.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie have kissed as directed in Dee's play. Dee evaluates the performance against her overwrought stage direction.
jokes.punchline: Dee's stage note is hilariously purple prose — 'quivering lips, juices of passion' — and her flat assessment that their kiss did not look like this, followed by 'So do that, then,' requires them to kiss again with more passion.
jokes.explanation: The gap between Dee's florid self-serious stage direction and the reality of Mac and Charlie being forced to kiss is very funny. 'Juices of passion' is specifically bad writing that Dee is fully committed to. 'Gladly' as Mac or Charlie's response to the direction to kiss better adds a layer of unexpected enthusiasm.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: with the quivering lips of two souls desperate to taste the juices of passion

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie backstage after being forced to kiss: 'Goddamn bitch.' 'She's sick is what she is.' 'And I know we're supposed to be cool with this 'cause that's where society's headed, but I'm just not there. I'm not ready.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie have just been forced to kiss each other on stage in Dee's play.
jokes.punchline: Their outrage is framed not as homophobia per se but as a generational/social discomfort — 'I'm not saying it's not right. I'm not ready.' Then: 'What did you eat? Why am I getting a weird taste...' 'I had cheese.'
jokes.explanation: Great multi-layered beat. 'That's where society's headed but I'm not ready' is a funny way to frame forced male kissing, especially given Mac's established character arc around repressed sexuality. The cheese detail is pitch-perfect gross-out that punctures the philosophical framing. 'Well, now you know how it feels' is Dee's perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: And I know we're supposed to be cool with this, 'cause, like, that's where society's headed, but I'm just... I'm not there.

jokes.text: Mac: 'What did you eat? Why am I getting a weird taste...' Charlie: 'I had cheese.' Mac: 'Well, now you know how it feels.' Charlie: 'Oh, I don't want to taste your cheese. It's weird...' Mac: 'Well, I didn't want to taste your cheese, either.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie have just kissed
jokes.punchline: They immediately dissect each other's taste, devolving into a mundane complaint about cheese — the intimacy of the kiss reduced to a flavor dispute
jokes.explanation: The cheese-taste complaint after a forced kiss is a perfect absurdist-mundane pivot. 'Well, I didn't want to taste your cheese, either' is a great mirror line. The domesticity of the exchange undercuts the drama in a very IASIP way.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Well, now you know how it feels.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, I don't want to taste your cheese.

jokes.text: Dee announces the next scene: Martina enters Tammy's massage parlor 'looking for a full-body rubdown... and like all great plays, this one is going to have a happy ending.'
jokes.setup: Dee is introducing the next scene of her play while the guys are already miserable.
jokes.punchline: 'Like all great plays, this one is going to have a happy ending' — using 'happy ending' in its massage parlor double entendre meaning, confirming the play is going to get more degrading.
jokes.explanation: Classic double entendre deployed cleanly. The characters' horrified reactions ('What?! Yeah. Oh, yeah.') sell it. Not particularly original but executed well.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: The ostrich's eyes are bigger than its brain. Do you have any thoughts on that?

jokes.text: Frank staggers back after the valet disaster: 'Yeah, that was clams.'
jokes.setup: Frank has spent the entire episode insisting 'The clam is fine' and 'It's not the clams.'
jokes.punchline: After vomiting explosively in front of the councilwoman, Frank returns and simply says: 'Yeah, that was clams.' — full capitulation, three words, no elaboration.
jokes.explanation: Among the episode's very best jokes. After an entire episode of Frank insisting 'The clam is fine' / 'It's not the clams!' / 'It won't be clams' — the full surrender rendered in exactly three words: 'Yeah, that was clams.' Perfect economy (10/10), perfect structure (the arc from denial to confession), perfect character voice. This is what 'maximum funny per word' looks like. Absolutely quotable. This is a 9+ moment.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, my God, I want to scream 'bird,' I want to scream 'bird.' That would be so good.

jokes.text: Bird-watching scene: Dee says ostriches have eyes bigger than their brains. The guys respond 'That's cool,' 'Good bird,' 'Great bird,' 'Ostriches are good birds.'
jokes.setup: The gang is forced to go bird-watching with Dee, performing interest in birds.
jokes.punchline: Their hollow, interchangeable affirmations — 'Cool,' 'Good bird,' 'Great bird,' 'Ostriches are good birds' — reveal they have absolutely nothing to say but are trying to appear engaged.
jokes.explanation: Light but effective. The escalating meaninglessness of 'Good bird. Great bird. Ostriches are good birds.' captures the gang's performative engagement perfectly. Bonus: the ostrich fact (eyes bigger than brain) has an obvious implication about Dee that the show wisely leaves unspoken.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Charlie has been outshining me all day, and I want to shine for you, Dennis

jokes.text: The moment Dee leaves for the bathroom, Dennis says 'Oh, my God, I want to scream bird, I want to scream bird!' 'That would be so good.' 'Do you want me to do it for you, Dennis?' 'No. Don't do it. She's probably hiding behind a tree.'
jokes.setup: The gang has been suppressing their 'Dee's a bird' habit all day.
jokes.punchline: Dennis nearly breaks the moment she steps away. His anguish at suppressing the bird insult, Mac's offer to do it on his behalf, and Dennis's paranoid 'she's probably hiding behind a tree' all land perfectly.
jokes.explanation: Good running gag payoff. The idea that the gang is in physical discomfort from not being able to call Dee a bird is funny. Mac offering to absorb the violation on Dennis's behalf is a sweet moment of their friendship.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I haven't been outshining you. I was just throwing you looks because I wanted the candy, but I was gonna share it with you

jokes.text: Mac reveals he's been acting weird because Charlie was 'outshining' him. Charlie: 'I haven't been outshining you. I was just throwing you looks because I wanted the candy, but I was gonna share it with you.'
jokes.setup: Mac has been off his game all episode, jealous that Charlie seemed to be getting Dennis's approval.
jokes.punchline: The grand rivalry Mac imagined — Charlie outshining him, trying to replace him, complex interpersonal scheming — was entirely in his head. Charlie was just trying to get candy.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional structural payoff. Mac's entire paranoid spiral about being outshone and replaced — his complex interpersonal fears — collapses against Charlie's completely pure motivation: candy, which he was going to share anyway. The gap between Mac's melodrama and Charlie's simple goodness is the joke, and it retroactively makes both confessionals funnier. 'I was gonna share it with you' is an unexpectedly touching detail that makes Charlie even more Charlie. High rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I keep candy in my pocket sometimes so that I can get Charlie's focus. It was working like a charm, man.

jokes.text: Dennis reveals he keeps candy in his pocket specifically to manage Charlie's focus: 'I keep candy in my pocket sometimes so that I can get Charlie's focus. It was working like a charm, man.'
jokes.setup: The gang confronts Dennis about the candy Charlie detected.
jokes.punchline: Dennis admits he has been conditioning Charlie like a dog with pocket candy — casually, as a standard leadership tool — 'working like a charm.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect character reveal. Dennis having a candy-conditioning system for Charlie — deployed casually, without shame — is both funny and deeply Dennis: he's an aspiring manipulator who treats people as systems to be managed. The fact that Charlie was 100% right about the candy (and that it worked perfectly) makes Charlie's detective work even funnier retroactively.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'll bang her as fast as I possibly can, and then, while she's cleaning up afterwards, I'll set all of her clocks back

jokes.text: The gang distributes the candy: 'Are we gonna get the candy?' 'Here's the candy.' 'Yeah! Yes! I knew it!' — with what is clearly chaotic grabbing.
jokes.setup: Dennis admits to the candy and the gang demands their share.
jokes.punchline: Four grown men — mid-elaborate political conspiracy — dissolve into excited scrambling for hard candies. Dennis's flat 'Children. Children.' is the button.
jokes.explanation: The candy payoff is satisfying. 'Children.' from Dennis — the man who was using candy to train Charlie — is the perfect ironic button. He created this dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I'm talking about the concealer, yes. But I'm talking about the rest of the makeup, the tape you have behind your jaw and your eyes. I'm talking about the hair paint.

jokes.text: Dennis's backup plan: 'I'll peel off. I'll go seduce her. She'll invite me into her house, where I'll bang her as fast as I possibly can, and then, while she's cleaning up afterwards, I'll set all of her clocks back.'
jokes.setup: The key-based plan has collapsed. Dennis announces an alternative.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's backup plan is to seduce the councilwoman, have sex 'as fast as possible,' and then reset her clocks during her post-sex cleanup — presented as a totally reasonable tactical pivot.
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis: his seduction skills are the most reliable tool in the gang's toolkit, to be deployed for even mundane political manipulation. 'As fast as I possibly can' undercuts his usual sexual vanity — it's purely functional. Very Dennis.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: That's what his soul looks like.

jokes.text: Dee takes Dennis to a nice restaurant and strips off his concealer, jaw tape, eye tape, hair paint — his entire physical maintenance regime — in public.
jokes.setup: Dennis claims he needs to take a bathroom break to execute his plan.
jokes.punchline: Dee produces makeup wipes and forces Dennis to remove his concealer, then — when he admits to 'a little concealer' — reveals she knows about all of it: the jaw tape, eye tape, hair paint. All in a public restaurant.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a great Dee moment of genuine power. The escalation — concealer → tape behind the jaw → tape behind the eyes → hair paint → 'all of it' — demolishes Dennis's carefully maintained vanity image piece by piece. Dennis's fumbling partial admissions ('I mean, I'm wearing a little bit of concealer') are perfectly played. The reveal that Dennis's perfect face is a construction is high-value character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Do you like hard candy? I have candies. Oh, you know what? Actually, I don't. Scratch that. I threw all the hard candies at those idiot children.

jokes.text: Dee brings Dennis (now stripped of his beauty routine) to a nice restaurant and offers to introduce him to ladies: 'Would you like to go introduce yourself to some ladies?' Dennis: 'No... I'm okay.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just had all his cosmetic enhancements removed and is in a public restaurant full of attractive people.
jokes.punchline: Dee offers to bring women over to Dennis — his greatest wish in any other circumstance — and Dennis quietly declines. His vanity fully punctured.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in what Dennis doesn't say. His entire identity is built around being desired by women, and here, stripped of his maintenance, he quietly opts out. 'No... I'm okay.' is devastating for a character this vain. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Can I get your house key? We don't have to have sex like this. I can put another man's face on.

jokes.text: Dee offers to 'go round up' some ladies and bring them to Dennis. Dennis, stripped of his usual appearance, says quietly: 'No. Uh, I-I'm okay. Uh, no.'
jokes.setup: Dee offers Dennis his usual opportunity — approaching women — in his now-unenhanced state
jokes.punchline: The Golden God declines quietly, the first time we've seen his confidence genuinely deflated
jokes.explanation: The deflated 'No. Uh, I-I'm okay' from normally-supremely-confident Dennis is a great character beat. His identity is so tied to his appearance that losing the enhancements has genuinely reduced him. Good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: This man is clearly a monster, and he will be punished accordingly.

jokes.text: Mac sees the councilwoman in the restaurant and encourages Dennis: 'Makeup or not, you are the Golden God. It's all about what's in here.' Then: 'Oh. Is your pec deflated?'
jokes.setup: Mac is giving Dennis an inspiring speech about inner confidence.
jokes.punchline: Mid-pep-talk, Mac spots that one of Dennis's pec pads is missing or deflated — Dee apparently removed those too — which completely undercuts the inspirational moment.
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic timing. Mac's sincere 'It's all about what's in here' speech — genuinely trying to help Dennis — is immediately destroyed by noticing a deflated pec pad. The juxtaposition of inner-beauty speech with the discovery of chest padding is very funny. 'Oh. Is your pec deflated?' is a great line — the 'Oh.' of gentle surprise is perfect. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: News anchor
dialogue.line: In a stunning upset, local ordinance LC-103 passed today. The controversial proposal actually legalizes public urination.

jokes.text: Mac's final pep talk: 'Well, either way, man, you can do it. You're our only hope.' Then the guys watch Dennis walk toward the woman: 'He ain't got this.' 'That's what his soul looks like.'
jokes.setup: The gang sends Dennis off to seduce the councilwoman.
jokes.punchline: The moment Dennis walks away, everyone drops the encouraging facade: 'He ain't got this.' Then Charlie or Frank adds: 'That's what his soul looks like' — presumably about Dennis's deflated, stripped-down appearance.
jokes.explanation: 'That's what his soul looks like' is a great line — it simultaneously refers to Dennis's deflated physical appearance and implies something true about his interior. Good economy with real punch.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Why didn't you just go and slash her tires, like, five minutes before she had to leave for the meeting?

jokes.text: Dennis's disastrous seduction attempt: 'Hi. Did I frighten you? Sorry. I'm not, I'm not, uh... I'm Dennis.' Long pause. 'Do you like hard candy? I have candies. Oh, you know what? Actually, I don't. Scratch that.'
jokes.setup: Dennis, stripped of his physical enhancements and unmoored from his usual persona, attempts to introduce himself to the councilwoman.
jokes.punchline: His opening is stammered and broken. Then he pivots to offering candy — his actual power move with Charlie — before realizing he already gave it all away. The unraveling of Dennis's seduction toolkit in real time.
jokes.explanation: Excellent cringe comedy. Dennis Reynolds — the self-proclaimed Golden God — is reduced to 'I'm Dennis' with a confused pause, then attempts to deploy his candy trick only to remember he gave it all away. The layers here are exceptional: Dee stripped his face, the candy's gone, and his self-concept has completely crumbled. The callback to both the candy arc and the makeup deconstruction make this land harder. One of the best Dennis moments in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: My plan did work, jackass. I got close enough to the councilwoman in the restaurant to steal her wallet, got her address, and then replaced the wallet without her seeing

jokes.text: Dennis offers the councilwoman candy: 'Do you like hard candy? I have candies. Oh, you know what? Actually, I don't. Scratch that. I threw all the hard candies at those idiot children.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is attempting to charm the councilwoman and reaches for his candy
jokes.punchline: He offers candy, then immediately reveals he already threw it at children in a fit of rage — the candy that was supposed to control Charlie, now weaponized against children
jokes.explanation: 'I threw all the hard candies at those idiot children' is a great absurdist revelation. The candy — previously established as Dennis's control mechanism — has apparently been used as projectile ammunition against children in his frustration. This is both a great callback payoff and a revealing Dennis moment. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Did you see how many times I peed today? I have a teeny, tiny, little bladder. I want to be able to pee on the street if I have to.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Oysters or clams?' Councilwoman: 'Excuse me?' Dennis: 'Oysters, obviously. You know?' Then he goes on about clams making you sick, mentioning Frank throwing up — 'He's not really my dad, but you know.'
jokes.setup: Dennis, in full panic, is trying to make conversation with the councilwoman he's meant to seduce.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's desperate gambit is to initiate the shellfish debate — the most absurd possible icebreaker — then segues into Frank vomiting, then clarifies Frank 'isn't really his dad.' Each beat is worse than the last.
jokes.explanation: Perfect collapse of Dennis's seduction toolkit. That the shellfish debate — which derailed the planning session — is now Dennis's pickup line is a great structural callback. 'Oysters, obviously' as a seduction opener is the kind of confident wrongness that only Dennis would attempt. 'He's not really my dad, but you know' is the detail that breaks the moment entirely.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You should all probably check your phones. Just 'cause I pushed the cuckoo clock ahead an hour

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Hey, uh, you know what? I just realized. We don't have a lot of time, so let's... we should get this over with. Can I get your house key? We don't have to have sex like this. I can put another man's face on.'
jokes.setup: Dennis's seduction has gone nowhere and he's running out of time.
jokes.punchline: He drops the pretense entirely and just asks for her house key, then offers to have sex with her but wearing 'another man's face' — apparently a literal option he has.
jokes.explanation: 'I can put another man's face on' is one of the episode's best lines — deeply disturbing, completely Dennis, and delivered as a reasonable accommodation. The offer to wear someone else's face as a favor mid-failed seduction is high-caliber dark comedy. The 'we should get this over with' gives it the utilitarian framing that makes it land perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You just insulted me on Dee Day. You know what that earns you? Another day of Dee.

jokes.text: Dee steps in to 'rescue' the councilwoman from Dennis: 'This man is clearly a monster, and he will be punished accordingly. Go wait for me over there, monster.' Dennis obeys. 'We'll find another woman.' Dennis: 'It's Dee Day.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has spectacularly failed to seduce the councilwoman.
jokes.punchline: Dee publicly calls Dennis a 'monster,' banishes him ('Go wait for me over there, monster'), and he COMPLIES — because it's Dee Day. His resigned 'It's Dee Day' as justification for obeying is perfect.
jokes.explanation: Excellent use of the Dee Day mechanic. Dennis Reynolds being publicly called a 'monster' by his sister and walking to a corner like a scolded child — justified only by 'It's Dee Day' — is a great reversal of his usual position in the group. 'Go wait for me over there, monster' is quotable and perfectly delivered.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Just so you know, you look... a lot better now, but you looked fine. I just don't look good when I haven't got enough sleep. And I got a little nap in, so, you know, I'm back.'
jokes.setup: Dee Day is almost over and Dennis is reclaiming his self-image.
jokes.punchline: Dennis offers a backhanded compliment to Dee while simultaneously assuring himself — without prompting — that he 'just needed a nap' and is now 'back.' Refusing to acknowledge that the makeup and pads were doing anything.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dennis denial — his terrible performance without his face work is rationalized as a 'sleep thing,' and he announces he's 'back' unprompted. His entire identity won't allow him to process what just happened. Great character consistency.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Oh, man. That's, like, the 20th piss I took today.' — referencing the bathroom-break plan system.
jokes.setup: Dee Day is almost over; the gang is waiting for the news
jokes.punchline: Mac has apparently urinated twenty times as part of their 'take a shit as cover' plan — the system worked against them more than for them
jokes.explanation: Minor callback that gets a mild laugh — the scheme's unintended consequence. Not particularly sophisticated but functional.

jokes.text: Dee Day ends at noon; the moment it hits, the guys explode into the news, screaming for channel 7.
jokes.setup: Dee counts down the end of Dee Day.
jokes.punchline: The instant it hits zero, the gang explodes into their actual agenda — news channel, TV remote, shouting — revealing the entire day of performative civility has been a dam about to burst.
jokes.explanation: Good punctuation on the Dee Day conceit — the relief of the gang reverting to form is satisfying. Not a joke with a lot of craft but good structural release.

jokes.text: News broadcast: local ordinance LC-103 — public urination — has passed. The gang erupts in celebration: 'It passed! It passed!'
jokes.setup: The gang failed at every step of their elaborate plan to influence a city council vote
jokes.punchline: The ordinance passes anyway — their spectacular failure was irrelevant
jokes.explanation: Classic IASIP structure — the gang fails but gets what they wanted through no effort of their own. The reveal of what the ordinance actually is (public urination) recontextualizes the entire episode's stakes perfectly.

jokes.text: The gang explains the elaborate plan to Dee: set the councilwoman's clocks back so she sleeps late and misses the city council vote to legalize public urination.
jokes.setup: Dee asks what the gang has been scheming about all day.
jokes.punchline: The elaborate plan — fake sick child, impersonating valets, seducing a politician, stealing house keys, resetting clocks — was all to legalize public urination. The reveal of the goal deflates the grandeur of the plan.
jokes.explanation: Great payoff to the episode's A-plot mystery. The audience has been watching an Ocean's Eleven style heist all episode and the goal is the right to pee in public. The gap between the complexity of the plan and the smallness of the goal is the joke, and the reveal lands well.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Women will never understand what it's like to be a man. We just need to piss in public, okay? We need to hatch plans that actually work. Dee, your plan would not have worked.'
jokes.setup: Dee points out the whole complex plan was unnecessary.
jokes.punchline: Dennis dismisses her with 'Women will never understand what it's like to be a man' and 'we need to piss in public' — delivered as deep masculine truth — before insisting her (simpler, working) plan would not have worked.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's misogynistic confidence immediately before being proven wrong is well-constructed irony. The setup for Dee's reveal.

jokes.text: Dee reveals she spent Dee Day: stealing the councilwoman's wallet to get her address, replacing the wallet without being noticed, and sneaking out at night to slash her tires — all while the guys thought she was taking bathroom breaks.
jokes.setup: The gang dismisses Dee's capability while congratulating themselves on surviving Dee Day.
jokes.punchline: Dee reveals a complete parallel competence narrative — she executed a simpler, more effective version of their plan during the same day, using their 'taking a shit' cover story against them.
jokes.explanation: The episode's structural crown jewel. Everything recontextualizes: Dee's 'bathroom breaks' were missions, her 'bird-watching' positioned her near the councilwoman, and her Dee Day forced the gang to stay compliant while she executed a better plan. It retroactively makes the whole episode funnier on rewatch. The twist that Dee also wants to pee in public — and has a teeny tiny bladder — is the perfect final layer. This is excellent sitcom writing.

jokes.text: Dee explains why she cares about legalizing public urination: 'Did you see how many times I peed today? I have a teeny, tiny, little bladder. I want to be able to pee on the street if I have to.'
jokes.setup: The gang is stunned that Dee also had a plan. Frank asks why she did it.
jokes.punchline: Dee's motivation is revealed to be identical to the guys' — she needs to pee in public. All her Dee Day activities were cover for her own mission, and her reason is the gloriously undignified 'teeny, tiny, little bladder.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect retroactive payoff. Every time Dee said she needed to pee, we now realize it was both true (tiny bladder, her whole motivation) and cover for her missions. 'Teeny, tiny, little bladder' as the linchpin of the entire episode's conspiracy is brilliant deflation. The recontextualization of all her bathroom trips is very rewatchable.

jokes.text: The gang's horrified reaction to learning Dee wants to pee in public: 'In front of us?' 'Just out there in the public?' 'A woman? Squat?' 'Dee, you nasty.' 'Nasty.'
jokes.setup: Dee reveals she wants to pee in public.
jokes.punchline: The gang — who has been plotting all day for this exact right — is horrified that a woman would want the same thing. Their responses reveal a sexist double standard delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Great irony punchline. The gang immediately applies a gender double-standard without noticing, calling Dee 'nasty' for wanting exactly what they spent the whole day scheming for. The overlapping 'Nasty' at the end is a perfect button. It's pointed social comedy that's also very funny.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Dee, you spent the entirety of Dee Day coming up with a plan that eventually led to us getting exactly what we want, so... We scored. You're a stupid bird.'
jokes.setup: Dee has just revealed she outsmarted all of them.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's response is to claim credit — 'we scored' — and immediately revert to calling her a stupid bird, completely denying Dee her victory while simultaneously benefiting from it.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dennis. He refuses to give Dee any credit for outsmarting everyone, reframes her competence as incidental to 'us' winning, and immediately resorts to 'stupid bird.' This encapsulates the whole gang's relationship with Dee — she succeeds, they take credit, they still call her a bird. Highly quotable, great character integration.

jokes.text: Dee drops the final twist: she pushed their cuckoo clock ahead an hour, so when they insulted her post-Dee-Day, it was still technically Dee Day. 'Here's the problem, guys. You just insulted me on Dee Day. You know what that earns you? Another day of Dee.'
jokes.setup: The gang is celebrating the end of Dee Day and reverting to bird insults.
jokes.punchline: Dee reveals she set the cuckoo clock ahead — Dee Day wasn't actually over — meaning all their insults count. Another Dee Day is added. Callback to the 'tack another day on' rule from the opening.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional cold close. Dee uses the same clock-manipulation that was the gang's plan against them, and it works because she anticipated their insults the moment Dee Day ended. The rule (tack on a day for insults) was established in the opening — now it closes the episode. It's structurally tight, calls back to both the Dee Day rules AND the gang's clock scheme, and the gang's horror ('No. Shut up. No, no, no, no, no!') is perfectly earned. Best closing joke of the episode.

tmdb_overview: The Guys are in the final preparation stage for an unknown scheme when Dee excitedly enters to inform them that today is “Dee Day.” The guys have to do everything she wants without complaint.
